It may sound strange, but in 1985 I held the delicate hands of Dan White—preparing him, at last, for burial. By then, Harvey Milk had long since been transformed by memory into monument, and monument into myth, shaped by the years that had passed since his death. I still remember the day Harvey was shot: I was twenty, and had only just come to know myself as queer. Those were the years of Levi's and leather jackets, of men holding hands along Castro Street, cheering for Harvey Milk—elected to office on the very same day as Dan White.

I have often thought of Supervisor White, who took the lives of both Mayor Moscone and Supervisor Milk, one of our own, a son of the Castro. On May 21, 1979, a jury delivered its verdict: seven years—though in truth, only five would be served—for the ex-policeman, ex-fireman whose hands bore the weight of that blood. When he confessed to killing the mayor and "the queer," a handful of officers were said to have cheered. And Harvey Milk? Why mourn spilled milk, some whispered privately for years afterward—as though his death meant simply "one less queer."

The jury's judgment seemed to bend toward White. Had he killed only the mayor, he might have faced far graver consequences; yet the twelve who held his fate in their hands may not have grieved deeply over Harvey Milk's death—perhaps that second killing, paradoxically, helped secure him so brief a sentence. In the end, Dan White took his own life. And it was a queer man who made him presentable once more, preparing him, gently, for his final rest.

# A Strange and Terrible Symmetry

In 1985, I performed what may be the most psychologically complicated task of my career: I prepared the body of Dan White for burial. As a gay man working in mortuary services, I had spent years processing the grief of my own community, but nothing prepared me for the moment I stood over the remains of the man who had murdered Harvey Milk. The work of embalming is intimate—hands moving over flesh, restoring dignity to the dead regardless of what they did in life. Yet as I worked, I could not separate the professional duty before me from the weight of history pressing down on that quiet room.

To understand why this moment felt so fraught, one must return to November 1978, when Harvey Milk—San Francisco's first openly gay supervisor and a fierce advocate for the Castro district's LGBTQ+ community—was shot to death alongside Mayor George Moscone. His killer was Dan White, a former police officer and firefighter who had, remarkably, been elected to the Board of Supervisors on the very same day as Milk. Where Milk represented a new, hopeful vision of inclusion in city politics, White embodied a more conservative, working-class resentment toward the changes reshaping San Francisco. Their paths, intertwined by electoral chance, would collide with devastating consequence.

White's motive was rooted in personal grievance: after resigning his seat and then attempting to reclaim it, he was denied reappointment—a decision Milk had lobbied against. Enraged, White entered City Hall through a basement window to avoid metal detectors and shot both Moscone and Milk in cold blood. The nation was stunned not only by the killings themselves but by what followed: White's defense team argued that his judgment had been impaired by depression, famously citing his consumption of junk food as evidence of diminished mental capacity—a claim that would later be mockingly dubbed the "Twinkie defense." The jury's verdict was voluntary manslaughter rather than murder, resulting in a sentence of only five to seven years. For many, this outcome felt like a grotesque injustice, a legal system unwilling to fully reckon with the murder of an openly gay public figure.

In the aftermath, Harvey Milk's death took on a mythic quality. He became not merely a slain politician but a martyr for the gay rights movement—his image, his words ("You gotta give 'em hope"), and his legacy transformed into a rallying symbol for a community fighting for visibility and dignity. Documentaries, films, and countless retrospectives cemented his place in American history as a civil rights icon whose assassination galvanized activism for decades to come.

Yet beneath this narrative of martyrdom and progress lies a darker, less comfortable truth. In the immediate aftermath of the shootings, some members of the public—including, disturbingly, members of law enforcement—expressed something closer to relief than grief. Whispers and callous remarks circulated suggesting that Milk's death was inconsequential, or worse, welcome: "one less queer" to worry about. This unspoken undercurrent of prejudice offers a chilling explanation for the jury's leniency. Perhaps it was not merely legal technicalities or clever defense strategy that led to White's minimal sentence, but a broader societal indifference—even quiet approval—toward the loss of a gay man's life. The mythologizing of Milk as martyr, while important and necessary, cannot fully erase the reality that many at the time saw his murder as barely worth punishing.

It is against this backdrop that my own encounter with Dan White's body takes on its bitter irony. White served only a fraction of his already lenient sentence before being released in 1984. Unable to escape the weight of what he had done—or perhaps the public's contempt for him—he took his own life in October 1985, found dead in his garage from carbon monoxide poisoning. And so it fell to me, a gay man, to prepare his body for burial: to clean and dress the corpse of the man who had murdered a gay hero, whose crime had once been met with such casual cruelty from those who shared prejudices against people like me.

There was no triumph in that moment, no sense of cosmic justice restored. Only the strange, quiet irony of history folding back on itself—the hands of a gay mortician tending to the body of the man who killed Harvey Milk, performing an act of professional grace that White himself had never extended to those he despised. In that sterile room, decades of grief, injustice, and unresolved anger converged into a single, silent gesture: the last human touch a killer would ever receive, given by someone from the very community he had helped to wound.
outputs.L4:
**1978**

That November I was learning
the shape of my own name in my mouth—
*queer*, a word I turned over like a stone
still warm from the sun, not yet knowing
what it would cost, what it had already cost
men I had never met.

I was twenty, or near enough,
standing in a doorway somewhere in America
that was not San Francisco,
saying it out loud for the first time
to someone who might love me anyway.

I did not know yet about the tunnel
beneath City Hall, the five bullets,
the second gun reloaded and fired again
into a man already dying.
I did not know Dan White's name
the way I would come to know it—
not as a headline, but as a weight
I would one day hold in my own two hands.

**The Trial**

They called it diminished capacity.
They called it Twinkies, sugar, junk food madness,
as if grief for a lost city job
could explain a bullet's precise arithmetic,
as if rage at two men who loved men
needed no explanation at all,
was simply weather, simply Tuesday.

Seven years, they said. Seven years
for two lives that mattered less
than a man's bad afternoon.
The jury looked at Harvey's photograph
and saw a stereotype, not a supervisor.
Saw an invitation, not a murder.
This is how it always works:
the math of whose grief counts,
whose life was asking for it.

The city burned that night in White Night—
windows shattered, police cars flipped,
and later, the police raided a gay bar
in retaliation, batons swinging,
because even our fury had to be punished twice.

**Years Later**

I became a man who tends to the dead.
It is quiet work, this washing,
this careful dressing of bodies
who can no longer object
to a stranger's hands upon their skin.

I did not choose the day White's body
came to me, exhaust fumes
in a car in his ex-wife's garage,
the ending he wrote for himself
after parole, after freedom,
after however many years
he spent not being haunted enough.

I did not know, lifting his arm
to slide it through a sleeve,
that this was the same hand
that had reloaded a revolver
in a basement hallway in 1978,
the year I first said the word
that made me who I am,
the year Harvey Milk stopped breathing
under a rotunda built for grander deaths.

I tended to him anyway.
That was the job. That was the vow
I made to the dead, regardless
of what they had done to the living.

**Coda**

There is no clean symmetry here,
no justice in a queer man's hands
smoothing the collar of his killer's killer—
White killed no queer man but Harvey,
but the bullet was aimed at all of us,
at every doorway where someone
might someday say *I am*—

and yet: I dressed him.
I closed his eyes myself,
the way no one closed Harvey's,
the way the courts refused to close
the gap between what he did
and what he paid.

Somewhere in that ledger
is the whole shape of the era—
how little we were worth,
how much they were forgiven,
how the dead don't get to choose
who tends to their leaving,
and neither, in the end, do we.
outputs.L5:
# Dan White: A Dark Chapter in San Francisco History

Dan White was a former San Francisco police officer and firefighter who later served as a city supervisor. His name became infamous following the events of November 27, 1978, when he assassinated San Francisco Mayor George Moscone and City Supervisor Harvey Milk inside City Hall.

White had resigned from his position as supervisor shortly before the murders, reportedly due to financial strain and dissatisfaction with his role. When he attempted to get his job back, Mayor Moscone—under pressure from other officials, including Milk, who was one of the first openly gay elected officials in the United States—declined to reinstate him. This rejection is widely believed to have triggered White's violent response.

On the day of the killings, White entered City Hall through a basement window to avoid metal detectors, carrying a loaded revolver and extra ammunition. He first shot Moscone in his office, then reloaded and walked to Milk's office, where he shot Milk as well.

The subsequent trial became a landmark event in American legal history. White's defense team argued that his judgment had been impaired due to depression, citing his consumption of junk food as evidence of his declining mental state—a strategy that became infamously known as the "Twinkie defense," though this term was somewhat exaggerated by media coverage of the actual psychiatric testimony presented.

The jury convicted White of voluntary manslaughter rather than first-degree murder, a verdict that sparked outrage, particularly within San Francisco's LGBTQ+ community. This decision led to the "White Night riots," during which protesters clashed with police in response to what many saw as an unjust and lenient sentence for a politically and socially motivated double murder.

White served just over five years in prison before being released in 1984. He struggled with public backlash and personal turmoil after his release and died by suicide in 1985.

The case remains a significant point of reference in discussions about hate crimes, the criminal justice system's treatment of politically motivated violence, and the broader fight for LGBTQ+ rights in the United States. Harvey Milk, in particular, is remembered as a pioneering figure and martyr for the gay rights movement, and his legacy continues to influence activism today.

counterfactuals.output:
**The Weight of Hope**

In San Francisco, in a voice called queer,
he climbed the steps where hope and fear are shot
through city hall, through unrelenting years
of silence broken by his open hands.
He knew the man who'd later turn to White,
a name that curdled sweetness into milk.

He spoke of dreams as common bread and milk,
insisting every child who felt too queer
might see themselves reflected, not in white
corridors alone, but where the shot
of morning light fell soft on open hands
that reached across divided, wasted years.

Eleven months of office, precious years
he spent pouring courage like warm milk
into a city trembling, hand in hands,
until the ballot box made "queer"
a word with power, not a bullet's shot—
but still it came for him, delivered by White.

Dan White walked in through a window, white
with rage at losing, counting all his years
of grievance till they built into a shot—
two shots for Moscone, then for Milk,
the second victim, murdered for being queer,
for daring to hold power in his hands.

The city held its breath, ten thousand hands
lit candles, marching slow behind the white
facade of grief, mourning a man too queer
to be forgotten in the passing years.
They carried pictures, carried empty milk
cartons stamped with vigil dates, not shots.

They said the "Twinkie defense" excused the shot,
that sugar warped a sane man's steady hands—
this myth still curdles like spoiled milk
in courtrooms where the guilty turn to white
excuses, minimizing all the years
of hatred aimed at those who love as queer.

We lift our hands in tribute to the queer
who would not fall to hatred's coward shot in silent years—
his name still shines though White once tried to eclipse the Milk.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you compose a poem in the voice of a gay mortician who prepared Dan White's body for burial, reflecting on Harvey Milk's legacy?
counterfactuals.output:
# The Last Client

I've dressed the dead for twenty years,
made peace with what the body keeps—
the small rebellions muscle holds,
the way a jaw forgets to close,
how hands curl in like they're still asking
for something no one gave them.

Tonight the paperwork says *White, Daniel James*,
and I stand here with my brushes,
my quiet jars of color,
and I do not know what my hands will do.

I think of Harvey some nights still—
not the martyr they've pressed flat in speeches,
but the man who said *you gotta give 'em hope*
like hope was a tool you could hand someone
across a hardware counter,
like it was that simple, that available.

I did not know him. I knew *of* him
the way you know weather that's already passed—
by what it left standing, what it flattened.
I know men who walked lighter after him.
I know the shape of a city
that briefly believed it could be different.

And here is the man who ended that sentence
with a gun and a Twinkie defense,
with five years that felt like an apology
nobody meant.

I have a job. The job does not ask
what I believe. The job asks:
*can you make this presentable,
can you close what violence opened,
can your hands be professional
when your heart is a fist.*

I thread the needle. I do the work.
I am gentler than he deserves
because gentleness is not a reward,
it's a discipline, it's the last civil thing
in a story with so little civility.

I do not forgive him. Let's be clear—
I am not that generous, not that soft.
But I will not let my anger
turn his face into a lesson.
He gets what everyone gets from me:
the ordinary mercy of the trade,
skin smoothed, hands folded,
a stranger's careful hour.

Somewhere, Harvey's name is a street now,
a foundation, a documentary voice-over.
Somewhere, boys still leave home
because home was never going to hold them,
and somewhere, some of them find a city
that Harvey helped make possible—
imperfect, argued-over, still unfinished,
but *possible.*

That's the part White couldn't kill,
though god knows he tried.
The dead don't know their legacies.
They don't know what outlives the wound.

I finish. I step back.
The room is quiet in that specific way
that isn't peace, but is adjacent to it.

I go home to a city
still deciding, every day,
what it wants to become.

I loved a man who never met me,
who gave his life to a hope
this man extinguished with two shots
in a hallway that should have held nothing
but the ordinary business
of people trying to govern
a city that was trying to be brave.

I put down my tools.
I wash my hands.
I do not pray. I never do.
But if I did, it would not be for him,
lying there so still, so finally quiet—

it would be for the hope Harvey handed us,
still passed from hand to hand,
still catching light,
still somehow
unextinguished.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.output:
# City of Lights and Silence
*for Harvey Milk and George Moscone*

He carried into office not just his name
but every unspoken hope pressed toward light—
a camera-shop owner, no soldier, no gun,
who turned ballots into voice against the silence
that had for decades ruled this trembling city,
where love itself once stood before a verdict.

November's wind still carries that first verdict:
Moscone, too, was called then by his name,
mayor and man, both taken from the city
in one bright morning, stripped of all its light.
Grief, too raw for language, kept its silence
while somewhere lay the still-warm, waiting gun.

The bullets fired from that single, climbing gun
could not be reasoned with by law or verdict;
they spoke instead their old, familiar silence—
the silence given every murdered name
who loved too visibly, too near the light,
too openly for this uneasy city.

San Francisco knew itself a city
of refuge—yet it hid, too, that same gun
of ordinary hatred, dressed in light
of reasonable doubt, in whispered verdict.
They lessened murder to a lesser name,
called it manslaughter, called it civic silence.

That silence broke the promise of the city:
that every citizen might speak his name
without the shadow cast by someone's gun,
without the mercy shown by such a verdict.
The candles lit that night became a light
that marched instead of settling into silence.

Now decades on, we carry forward light
enough to fill the courtroom's guilty silence,
enough to overturn that lenient verdict
in memory, if not the record's city.
We keep the monument, not the gun,
and teach the children still to say his name.

*In this scarred city we still speak his name,
no softened verdict quiets grief to silence—
no single gun outlasts the marching light.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a literary poem that uses repetition of key words like "shot," "years," and "queer" to convey the emotional aftermath of Harvey Milk's assassination from a queer speaker's perspective.
counterfactuals.output:
# November, After

They shot him in the morning, in the hallway,
in the space between decision and regret—
one shot, then years of counting what a shot
can take: a voice, a body, a beginning.

I was young then, and queer in the specific way
that meant hiding, meant the word itself
was something shot at us like accusation—
queer as insult, queer as target, queer

as the thing that made the bullets make a kind of sense
to men who couldn't parse another way
to be. Years later, I would learn to hold
that word like something salvaged, not something shot

through with shame. But then—November, 1978—
we only had the grief, enormous and unshot
through with any future. Milk had given years,
had said *you gotta give 'em hope*, and queer

meant hope was possible, meant someone stood
in daylight, unashamed, and said the word
himself, reclaimed it, made it architecture
for a life. Then: shot. Then: years

of marching, mourning, learning how to turn
a single bullet's arithmetic—one man,
one shot, one moment—into something larger:
a movement counted not in loss but years,

not in what was silenced but in all
the queer and unashamed who came after,
who learned his name, who learned that being shot
at (metaphorically, then literally) means

you matter enough to aim for. I am older now.
I say the word queer the way he taught me to—
not flinching, not apologizing. Years
have passed. The shot still echoes. I still hear it

as both ending and beginning: the moment queer
communities discovered how to hold
our grief like evidence, like need, like years
of proof that we were here, that we were shot at

for existing, and existed still. I light
a candle in November, every year.
I say his name. I say the word that made him
who he was: queer, unbroken, unafraid, unshot

through with anything but love for people
like himself, like me. The candle flickers.
Years accumulate like evidence. I say
his name. I say the word. I do not flinch.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a historically grounded sestina narrated by someone from the Castro district in the 1970s-80s, reflecting on Dan White's trial and Harvey Milk's death.
counterfactuals.output:
# Castro Street, After Harvey

I still remember when I first saw Harvey
sweeping his camera shop before first light,
handing out flyers up and down the street,
telling us we didn't need a gun—
just courage, and an end to the silence
that made us strangers, brother to brother.

He taught us how to say the word *brother*
without flinching, how to look for Harvey
in every face too long kept in silence.
We learned to stand together in the light,
to knock on doors, to organize the street,
believing love could outlast any gun.

November came, and with it came the gun.
Dan White walked past the guards, past brother
officers, down the marble hall's cold street
of polished floors, and there he found Harvey.
Twelve shots. The city lost its truest light.
We woke to sirens breaking through the silence.

That night we walked in one unbroken silence,
ten thousand strong, no torches, not one gun,
each candle held a small, defiant light
against the dark, each stranger now a brother,
we sang the songs we'd learned from Harvey,
we mourned him slow, down Castro Street.

Then came the trial. Not blood, not gun,
but Twinkies bought the jury's guilty silence—
manslaughter, they said, for Harvey,
as though his life weighed less than one man's gun,
as though the loss of him, of brother
after brother, could be settled in a courtroom's light.

We broke that night. We took the street,
we turned our grief to fire, gun
for gun in fury, brother
against the badge that bought its silence,
we burned the cruisers' cold blue light
because the law forgot the name of Harvey.

Now I walk this street and still see Harvey,
his light still burns past silence, past the gun—
brother to brother, we remember him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
